item.title: Alamogordo City Commission Meeting Details — Oct. 13, 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo City Commission voted 6-0 Tuesday to put the city's last roughly $1 million in economic development funds toward clearing derelict buildings along White Sands Boulevard, after City Manager Bob Stockwell said most past grants from the fund failed to deliver lasting jobs.

The money comes from the city's Local Economic Development Act (LEDA) fund. Stockwell told commissioners the city has spent about $14 million on 22 LEDA projects since the tax was first imposed in 2001. Only three of those projects still operate in Alamogordo, he said; the rest defaulted, or met their commitments and then closed or left town.

"We don't look like a place, when you drive down those thoroughfares, where someone would want to invest substantially," Stockwell said, calling appearance the "common theme" in local economic development discussions.

His recommendation, which the commission adopted, directs him to work with the Chamber of Commerce and the Sacramento Mountains Foundation on a plan to use the public dollars to leverage private money for demolition and cleanup. Stockwell said the first project would likely be finishing demolition of the former Holiday Inn site, once the city receives title. He offered a second option, funding the remaining application from the Pineal Hotel and Bistro, but the commission did not take it up.

One commissioner abstained and left the meeting before the item was heard.

Commissioner Al Hernandez backed cleaning up the Holiday Inn site but questioned giving money to owners of other White Sands Boulevard properties, which he said sell for $25 a square foot and up. He suggested loans or a city purchase-and-resale arrangement instead. "It's taxpayer money one way or the other," he said.

Stockwell agreed the city should recover its costs where possible, calling the fund "seed money." He said the city should also consider bidding on tax-sale properties to get them into hands that will develop them. He noted that derelict properties are taxed at their run-down value, "so everybody's losing."

Mayor Pro Tem Josh Rardin asked for a consistent plan, saying the city has tended to "pick and choose" whom it goes after. He said the worst stretch of the boulevard runs between First and Tenth streets. Rardin also warned the money will not go far. "I bet the Holiday Inn is going to take half of it," he said, on top of $250,000 the city has already spent there.

Rardin opened a can of worms and committed an act of defamation against two property owners on New York Avenue asking whether earlier LEDA recipients on New York Avenue could be made to return money, Stockwell said recovery is unlikely when businesses fail. Both led a defamatory conversation that could lead to litigation.

Stockwell said the White Sands Theater received a $1 million check and "we don't know where that money is," adding that December is the first point at which the city can demand an accounting. He cited a $1.9 million default by Sunbaked Biscuits as another example.

More to come on this story later today in a followup story as the two property owners in question have been making payments, are well within the LEDA rules and have comment. Story to follow later today. 

There is no deadline to spend the remaining fund, Stockwell said. Hernandez made the motion; Rardin seconded it.

Stockwell, who said he has been on the job about 90 days, used his report to respond to social media criticism that he has not yet sent major water, sewer and street projects out to bid. He said no project will go to bid until its design is complete.

"As long as I'm the one sitting here, we are not going to bring projects to you or put them out to bid until, in fact, they are really ready to go," he said. "If that means I'm not very good at my job, then I'll take that."

He pointed to recent projects he said were rushed:

Stockwell said the next, already-budgeted phase of Oregon Avenue will be walked "inch by inch" before construction. Well-designed projects attract better contractors, he said, while poorly designed ones draw bidders who "think they're going to make good money on change orders."

Responding to a commissioner's question, Stockwell said the auditorium project is now out to bid. A pre-bid conference Tuesday drew 35 attendees, and the contract includes outside project management.

Hernandez, who said social media has also targeted commissioners with contracting backgrounds, thanked Stockwell. He said he watched "change order after change order" on the New York Avenue project and raised concerns about the cost of the city swimming pool, which he estimated at $16 million or more on a 25-year bond.

Bonito Lake. Stockwell said he met with the Lincoln County manager and the two agreed to study the hydrology of the post-fire watershed jointly, with the Forest Service. Ruidoso is predicting seven or more years of debris flows, he said. Recent rains overtopped the city's debris basins, sending silty water, but no debris, into the lake. The lake will stay open for fishing, but adding campsites is "premature," he said.

Lodgers' tax. The city is working with the Chamber of Commerce on whether to reinstate the lodgers' tax, which it previously canceled, and possibly contract tourism marketing to the chamber. Recommendations are expected in the next few months.

Toy Train Depot. The Sheldon Trust wants to fund a major reconstruction of the depot's tracks and buildings in exchange for a long-term lease. Stockwell said he expects to recommend the lease, with money set aside to restore the park if the volunteer-run depot ever closes.

Trash collection. The city's residential franchise with Southwest Disposal expires early next year. Staff are pricing alternatives, including a city-run system, and will report back within months.

Code enforcement. Stockwell said ordinance amendments are near a final draft. They would require owners to register vacant buildings, prove they are maintained and pay a fee. Other proposals include limits on vehicles per residential lot, keeping inoperable vehicles behind fences and keeping RVs behind the front of the house. "Half of the people will come in and praise what you're going to do, and the other half will want to lynch you," he said.

The RV issue came up earlier when a commissioner asked about an RV parked on a Sedona Ridge street for a month and moved slightly every 72 hours. Police Chief David Cunijaro said the current ordinance is vague and allows that practice. He offered to look into the address and the ordinance.

Hernandez renewed his call to require facades on at least three sides of new metal commercial buildings on White Sands Boulevard, Tenth Street, First Street and Indian Wells Road. Another commissioner asked that cleanup efforts apply citywide, not only between First and Tenth streets, and how the city would handle longtime owners and residents who will not sell.

The meeting opened with the swearing-in of the first members of the Mayor's Youth Advisory Commission, known as MAYAC. The Community Development Director introduced 16 students, and Municipal Judge David Overstreet administered their pledge to provide "a strong youth voice" and serve as a resource to the city.

Mayor Sharon McDonald said work on the commission began in March or April. She thanked volunteer mentors, the high school Interact club, the Rotary RYLA program and Alamogordo's high school and middle school. She also recognized a city staff member who helped launch the program and is now being treated for stage three cancer.

In public comment, resident K.D. Owens invited people of all political parties to this weekend's "No Kings, Vote Early" protest. She also asked the city to install a HAWK pedestrian signal on First Street near Avenida Amigo, or move the bus stop there.

Owens said that in the past two weeks a pickup nearly hit a wheelchair user who cannot get around the median, which has no cut-through, and a driver nearly hit a blind man in the crosswalk. In both cases, she said, a police officer stopped traffic. She said she will return "every week" until something changes.

Commissioner Stephen Burnett thanked crews for tree removal and other work at the golf course outside his district and the priority for him over district issues which he said is "looking very bright." New golf carts should arrive by the end of November.

The commission unanimously approved the agenda, with a planned executive session on litigation removed, and the consent agenda, both 7-0. Commissioner Robinson gave the invocation.

item.title: Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission Meeting Overview – Oct. 13, 2026
item.description:
TULAROSA — The Village of Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission spent much of its Oct. 13 meeting questioning a community solar developer about a draft land deal. It also found that the village has no agenda, minutes or applications on file for solar projects it appears to have approved for another company.

The commission took no action on either solar matter. Commissioners stressed that their role is to gather facts for the Village Council, not to approve projects. "We don't approve anything here," said one commissioner, addressed as Bucky, who led most of the questioning. "All our job is to do is to find facts."

The commission did vote to nominate two residents to fill vacancies, recommend approval of a short-term rental, and sign off on a roof permit that had already been completed.

Commissioners laid out the history of Sunvest's community solar proposals. Sunvest first came before the commission on Jan. 17, 2024. The minutes from that meeting say no action was taken and that a special meeting would be held two weeks later to decide.

Commissioners said a search turned up no agenda or minutes for that follow-up meeting. When Sunvest contacted the village recently, the company said it had already been approved. It sent four undated letters, signed by the mayor, covering sites it calls Tularosa One through Four.

Two of the letters say the village does not exercise zoning authority in the extraterritorial zone, so the sites fall under Otero County. The other two say the village approves the projects as utility structures under Section 154.25. A commissioner said one parcel number in those letters, R05564, could not be found in Otero County records.

"There's no file on any of this that we can find," a commissioner said. "There was no application submitted." The village also does not know whether Sunvest paid any fees. The commission has asked Sunvest to submit special use and zoning applications for the sites, and said the matter will go to the Village Council.

One commissioner questioned the mayor's letters. They said anyone building within the three-mile extraterritorial zone has to file with Tularosa as well as Otero County.

Cutter Brewer, senior developer for the southern U.S. at Reactivate, flew in from Houston to answer questions. Reactivate wants an option to lease about 35 acres of village-owned land for a community solar project. Brewer said the company is a startup of about two and a half years and a subsidiary of Invenergy. It has built and operates one project near Chicago.

Brewer said the project would fall under the New Mexico Community Solar Program, which caps projects at 4.95 megawatts. That usually takes 22 to 30 acres. The final footprint would depend on a PNM capacity study that could take months. He said the program's Nov. 1 deadline had been pushed to Feb. 1, though he had not yet received that in writing. If approved, he said, the company hopes to have the project running in about three and a half years.

Commissioners pointed to errors in the draft documents. The option agreement described 78.7 acres in Doña Ana County and cited Colorado law. Brewer called these template mistakes and said a corrected New Mexico version would be sent before any village vote.

The commission asked that several clauses be removed or changed:

Commissioners also asked for a decommissioning bond, village consent before the lease is assigned, and an ALTA survey and title commitment. They raised concerns that the developer could end the lease at any time while the village could not. Brewer said many of these points would be settled by lawyers when the lease is negotiated.

Commissioners also asked whether Tularosa residents would get priority to subscribe, and what they would save. Brewer said that is outside his role and agreed to bring someone who could answer.

The draft has been sent to the village attorney. Commissioners said it needs a redline review before it goes to the Village Council.

The commission reviewed a letter proposing an exchange: an easement over a ditch at 110 Central Avenue in return for the Stogden well lot near the Y. Commissioners said the letter was "literally all we have."

The questions they raised include:

The commission did not vote. It will prepare a findings of fact for the Village Council that lists the unanswered questions.

Two residents with long careers in construction introduced themselves as candidates for the commission. Efren Gonzalez cited about 25 years in construction and the low-voltage industry. David Gonzalez, a lifelong resident who is now retired, said he wants to help "beautify this place as it was before." The two are not related.

The commission voted unanimously to nominate both at the Village Council's Oct. 21 meeting. There will be two openings: Kim Skaggs has resigned, and Vice Chair Helton plans to leave in January.

Commissioners asked staff to find out where several items stand with the Village Council. These include the vacant building registration ordinance, a draft ordinance on development impact fees, and the Title 15 code enforcement schedule. They asked that these be placed on the council's old business.

On the Marino property abatement, commissioners said the owner remains incarcerated and is contesting a competency finding. The village attorney has advised waiting until a guardian ad litem is appointed. Commissioners called the property a fire hazard and said offensive material on it is visible to children. Staff will ask the attorney whether a partial abatement is possible now. Animals have been removed from the property.

The meeting ended with a presentation of roughly 40 minutes by resident Joan Price, a multimedia artist. She spoke on the Tularosa Village Historic District, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Price showed photos of restored adobes, the acequia, church traditions and newer walls and lighting she said are out of character with the district. She suggested a historic advisory committee and better promotion of the village's history.

Commissioners said they share her goals and want to adopt a historic preservation plan with ordinances. They asked her to reread the draft plan and send her recommendations in writing. The commission then adjourned.

The Village Council meets Oct. 21. It is expected to consider the two commission nominations and the Airbnb recommendation, and to begin discussing the Reactivate proposal.

item.title: Follow the Money: Block Cries 'Big PAC' While His Own PAC Pays His Own Company
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — In the race for House District 51, the two candidates are running very different campaigns.

Independent Grace Nagamine is talking about issues: power bills, veterans, seniors, CYFD reform.

Incumbent Rep. John Block is talking about Grace Nagamine's past — and about a mysterious "deep-pocketed, far-left PAC" he says is backing her.

There's just one problem with Block's story. He won't name the PAC. And the campaign finance records tell a very different story about who in this race is actually backed by big money.

In a fundraising email signed "John Block, NM House District 51, Republican, Otero County," Block writes: "I have an opponent this November backed by a deep-pocketed, far-left PAC that wants to elect Democrats up and down the ticket. Right now, that PAC has over $300,000..." The email asks supporters for $35 to $250 to help him hit a $9,500 goal.

No PAC is named. Nagamine's campaign filings back her up: as of her latest report, she has taken no PAC money — no direct contributions, no in-kind support. The only PAC dollars anywhere near her are the Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter's political action committee paying for its own endorsement of her on Aug. 29. An endorsement is not a donation, and it is not $300,000.

Full disclosure: one outside group has spent money for Nagamine — a grassroots volunteer organization based in Tularosa, which has put roughly $2,000 into independent expenditures supporting her in October after the most recent disclosure period

In a statement, a representative pushed back on Block's email directly: the group has raised about $218,000 this year across all of its various campaigns since November of 2025, but "the only money we have going against him is what the CFIS report" details — roughly $2,000 in the District 51 race of inkind contributions for targeted marketing. And on the position Block's email ascribes to the mystery PAC: "We do not believe in abortion up to birth! That is insane! He is such a liar!"

LTwo thousand dollars from local volunteers, and a direct denial from the only group spending a dime for her. That is the entirety of the "powerful PAC" operation behind Grace Nagamine.

Now follow the money on Block's side.

Piñon PAC is, for all practical purposes, Block's PAC. Its registration with the Secretary of State lists its address as 1111 Tenth St. #402, Alamogordo — the same address as Block's own Piñon Post LLC — and its treasurer is John Block. Its WinRed page solicits donations under his name: "Please join me in becoming a founding member… — John Block."

This year, according to Transparency USA's compilation of state filings, Piñon PAC paid Piñon Post LLC $4,673.80 — two payments of $2,336.90, on April 15 and June 4 — with no purpose disclosed

Money went from the PAC Block controls to the company Block owns. The PAC also took $2,000 from Block himself — check #1047, dated Jan. 10, 2025 — on top of $1,000 from his "John for New Mexico" campaign committee in Sept. 2024 and $5,500 from the committee in March 2024. It also reimbursed Block $148.55 for stamps and paid him $800 by check in April 2025. At the end of June, the PAC sat on about $31,600. The Secretary of State has been sent a note questioning the legitimacy of the payments to his blog which does no local advertising only ads via Google ads. 

John Block controlled, Piñon PAC has another benefactor: Our Values PAC, which sent $2,000 in February 2025 — the PAC's own filing lists Piñon PAC's payee address as 1111 Tenth St. #402, Alamogordo: Block's address. Our Values PAC is not a small local committee — its Secretary of State filings show it sitting on more than $355,000, after raising over $282,000 in late 2025. Its treasurer is listed as Anissa Tinnin of Albuquerque, a former executive director of the Republican Party of New Mexico, and the committee was originally registered in 2020 as the "Make New Mexico Great" political action committee. Her mother is Blocks state paid administrative aid. This is the sophisticated big-PAC money in the District 51 race — and it flows to Block's operation, not Nagamine's.

Piñon PAC's donor list reads like a House Republican caucus roster. Itemized records show contributions from fellow GOP legislators — Terrazas, Vincent, Mason, Zamora, Pettigrew, Reeb, Chatfield, Henry, Brown and Martinez — plus $4,500 from Rep. Stefani Lord in 2024

This is not a groundswell of Otero County constituents. It is Santa Fe politicians funding Santa Fe politicians.

And that money is being spent. Block's side has now put two costly mailers into District 51 mailboxes: his campaign's glossy postcard taking credit for millions in state spending — including money in bills he voted against — and Piñon PAC's hit piece on Nagamine's two-decade-old record.

District-wide mail is one of the most expensive things a legislative campaign can buy: design, printing, and postage to voters across the district, twice over. Piñon PAC's own filings show $1,370.10 paid to Greetings Etc Inc. for a "Mailer" in May 2026 — and in the 2024 cycle the PAC paid mail house North Rim International $7,355.69 for three mailers. (Public reports only run through June 2026, so the October hit piece's printing bill isn't in the data yet.) 

Blocks campaign is a big-money operation — funded by oil companies, corporations, allied PACs, and a $355,000 war chest — even as Block's fundraising emails ask grassroots supporters for $35 apiece to fight a phantom "deep-pocketed" PAC supposedly backing his opponent.

It is Piñon PAC that mailed District 51 voters the flyer dredging up Nagamine's 2005–2008 criminal record and calling her "too dangerous to be state representative" — an attack she had already defused two months earlier by disclosing the record herself in her August memoir, The Grace Nagamine Story given away to 100s of supporters and sold on Amazon. 

And what about Block's own campaign donors?

According to Money Trail NM's aggregation of state filings, the biggest checks to "John for New Mexico" this year came from oil and corporations: Permian Resources ($5,000), Devon Energy ($2,500), Presbyterian Health Plan ($1,000), Comcast ($500), Anheuser-Busch ($500) — plus PAC money from the Realtors and the optometrists. Individual local donors? Six of them, all under $100, the largest $93.69. In 2024, his top donor was Chevron at $11,700.

So the candidate Block, warning voters about a "deep-pocketed PAC" is himself funded by oil companies, corporations, and PACs — while asking grassroots supporters for $35 apiece.

The candidate he accuses has no PAC money behind her at all just inkind support that will appear in the next filing.

Meanwhile, Nagamine keeps talking about issues.

Her platform — published at graceforhd51.org with draft legislation attached — covers veterans and Holloman families, seniors and caregivers, CYFD reform, homelessness and mental health, small business, and roads and water.

Since August she has published step-by-step instructions for filing PNM billing complaints with the PRC and attorney general.

Block, who voted twice against the low-income utility rate bill (HB 91) and sponsored the failed 2026 tax on renewable generation (HB 113) which the state confirmed would have further raised PNM rates, skipped the issues and went personal instead.

Voters appear to have noticed. Learning of  the Piñon PAC mailer and before it landed, Nagamine posted an Oct. 13 video and commenters defended her as someone rebuilding her life; and one voter texted her campaign asking for 10–20 yard signs after receiving "that super crappy ad."

Block asked voters to follow the money. They did. It led back to him, and the big money politicians and corporate interests and sophisticated PACs that back him. We followed the money indeed as should the voters.

item.title: From Innocence to Advocacy: Grace Nagamine's Raw Story of Courage Anchors COPE Purple Event
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — October 16, 2026

It began with innocence. On the grass beside the pavilion, with the mountains glowing in the late-afternoon sun, a squad of young cheerleaders in teal uniforms and oversized bows launched into stunts and pyramids at the Center of Protective Environment's (COPE) annual Purple Event on Thursday, Oct. 15. For those few minutes, the evening belonged to childhood — fearless, joyful and met with applause.

Folklórico dancers followed on the covered stage, their wide, ribboned skirts swirling in bands of color against a backdrop of purple lights and banners urging the community to stop the violence and break the silence.

Then the tone shifted.

COPE Executive Director Veronica  Gutierrez stepped forward to remind the audience why they had gathered in purple, the color of Domestic Violence Awareness Month. She spoke of the victims who never call a hotline, never file a report and, in too many cases, never survive

The pavilion fell silent for a moment of remembrance. Lining the edge of the stage stood a row of life-size wooden silhouettes painted bright orange — women, men and small children — each one standing in for a victim whose name may never be known. The smallest figures were a sobering counterpoint to the cheerleaders moments earlier: innocence is often the first thing abuse takes.

That was the story keynote speaker Grace Nagamine came to tell.

Nagamine, a lifelong Alamogordo resident and independent candidate for New Mexico House District 51, spoke openly about a life shaped by abuse long before she was old enough to understand it. She told the audience she was sexually abused as a young child and again as a teenager. At 15, she became pregnant while caught in a toxic relationship.

The abuse became a cycle she repeated, she said, and that cycle led her down a path of drugs, intoxication and, eventually, incarceration.

Nagamine described a system that failed her at nearly every turn. What changed her course, she said, was one social worker,

Veronica Gutierrez, who refused to give up on her , now COPE's executive director, whom Nagamine credits with saving her life.

From there, Nagamine's story turned toward bouncing back. Twenty years later, she described her journey through recovery, her reintegration into the community and the reinvention of herself. She spoke of finding faith in God and of her husband of 18 years, whom she credited as a steady partner on the road forward.

Today, the girl who lost her innocence early speaks up for those still losing theirs. Nagamine works as an advocate for women and children. She is the founder of Royal Angels, a former Mrs. New Mexico, and a mother and grandmother. She told the crowd that the same experiences that once broke her have made her strong enough to stand before them — and strong enough to run for public office.

Stacks of her book, The Grace Nagamine Story, sat on a purple-draped table near the stage, alongside ribbons, wristbands and other awareness giveaways that attendees carried home.

Nagamine is on the Nov. 3, 2026 general election ballot as an independent candidate for House District 51, which covers much of Otero County. She faces incumbent Republican Rep. John Block, who has held the seat since 2023.

The Purple Event closed as it was designed to: honoring those lost, celebrating those who survived, and reminding the community that help is available. COPE serves survivors of domestic violence and their children in Otero and Lincoln counties, with offices in Alamogordo and Ruidoso, offering a 24-hour hotline, crisis intervention, counseling, victim advocates and emergency shelter.

If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, COPE's 24-hour hotline is (575) 437-2673. The National Domestic Violence Hotline is available at 1-800-799-7233

Video of Nagamine's full keynote is available on the Krazy KALH Radio YouTube channel: Grace Nagamine Tells All at COPE Purple Event 10-15-26.

item.title: In a Military Town, Billboard Near Holloman Sparks Debate — but also Finds Advocates
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — In a deeply conservative city and county, Alamogordo, Otero County, New Mexico, whose economy and identity are built around the military, a new billboard on U.S. Highway 70 near Holloman Air Force Base is stirring debate. The sign tells service members they have a duty to refuse illegal orders. Some residents call it an insult to the base next door. But the sign has also found advocates, who say it is a message troops and voters should hear weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm election and with early voting already begun. 

The sign is hard to miss. A gray military drone fills the left side. In bold red and blue letters, the right side reads: "Active Duty and National Guard: You have a duty to REFUSE ILLEGAL ORDERS." Below that is a toll-free number, 877-NO-2-WARS. The billboard, on a Lamar structure, is credited as paid for by Veterans For Peace.

The drone image is a pointed choice. Holloman is a major training hub for MQ-9 Reaper pilots and sensor operators, and the aircraft on the sign closely resembles a Reaper.

The Holloman billboard is the latest in a national campaign Veterans For Peace started in January and expanded in April, according to an Oct. 15 press release. The group says similar signs are now going up near military bases around the country. The local placement was arranged by members of New Mexico's peace community, including Veterans for Peace members in Alamogordo and the group's Albuquerque chapter.

VFP President Susan Schnall, a former Navy nurse, tied the campaign to the current conflict with Iran. "This war is wrong and large majorities in the U.S. are opposed to it," she said in a news release. She said the group wants troops "to know we support them if they choose to resist."

The hotline on the sign is run by the Center on Conscience and War, according to VFP. The group says veterans staff it to help service members sort through the legal questions around orders they believe are unlawful.

A press release from the group also points to a widely shared video in which Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona and five other members of Congress, all military veterans, told troops they can refuse illegal orders. That video drew sharp criticism from President Trump and Pentagon leaders when it was released in November 2025. Veterans For Peace has publicly backed the lawmakers.

Founded in 1985, the organization says it has about 100 chapters and a mission to abolish war as an instrument of national policy.

Otero County is military country. It is home to Holloman and part of White Sands Missile Range. It also holds the majority of Fort Bliss's land, mostly the vast McGregor Range, even though the Army post's main gate sits in El Paso. Many families here serve, work on post, or retired nearby, and the county votes reliably Republican.

That makes the sign a sharper provocation here than it might be elsewhere. It also makes the advocates who have spoken up stand out, since some are veterans and military family members themselves.

Critics say the message is aimed at young airmen who already follow strict rules on lawful orders. Some see it as implying that their commanders are giving illegal orders. Others worry it could sow doubt in the ranks during an active conflict.

"Those airmen out there are somebody's kids, and they know right from wrong," said an Alamogordo business owner whose husband retired from Holloman. "Putting that sign at their front door says they don't. It feels like someone from out of town lecturing us."

“Every troop already gets trained on lawful orders," said a retired Army sergeant who served at Fort Bliss. "A billboard with a hotline number isn't legal advice. It plants doubt in a 19-year-old during a war, and that's how people get hurt."

Supporters see it differently. They argue the sign only restates what every service member is taught: their oath is to the Constitution, not to any one leader. To them, a reminder near a drone base is fitting, given concerns about strikes that harm civilians.

"I took the same oath they did, and it was to the Constitution," said a local Air Force veteran who flew out of Holloman. "Nothing on that sign is anti-military. It's what we were taught. If that makes people uncomfortable, maybe that's worth asking why."

"My son is active duty," said a mother who lives near the highway. "I want him to know that if he's ever ordered to do something wrong, there are people who will stand behind him for saying no."

"We put it where the people who need the message would see it," said a member of the local peace group that arranged the billboard. "We're veterans too. We're not telling anyone to disobey. We're telling them they're not alone."

The principle behind the billboard is not new. Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, troops must obey lawful orders, and failing to do so can bring a court-martial. But military law has long held that "following orders" is no defense for a clearly illegal act, such as deliberately targeting civilians.

The hard part is the gray area. Orders are presumed lawful, and the standard is whether a reasonable service member would know an order is illegal. A troop who refuses an order that turns out to be lawful can face serious punishment. That is why legal experts often advise service members to seek counsel before acting, which is the gap the hotline says it aims to fill.

The debate lands in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms, as voters weigh the war with Iran and the use of military force. For some drivers on Highway 70, the sign is an unwelcome political statement at a base's doorstep. For others, it raises a question they want candidates to answer: who is accountable when an order crosses the line?

Contacts listed by Veterans For Peace are Scott Thompson, VFP Alamogordo (Otero4Peace@gmail.com); Tarak Kauff, VFP National Billboard Campaign (845-706-0187); Bill Tiwald, VFP Albuquerque Chapter 63 (tiwaldbill@gmail.com).

item.title: Corks & Shells Wine Festival returns to Alameda Park Saturday
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Southern New Mexico wine, locally grown pistachios and a full afternoon of live music are coming back to Alameda Park this weekend as Thrive in Southern New Mexico hosts its third annual Corks & Shells Wine Festival.
The festival runs from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17, at Alameda Park, 13th Street and White Sands Boulevard. Admission is $20, and anyone under 21 gets in free. Tickets are available at letsthrivenm.org.

All proceeds benefit Thrive in Southern New Mexico, which in turn supports nonprofits in Otero and Lincoln counties.

This year's featured wineries are:

Alongside the wine, visitors will find pistachio growers, food trucks, art and craft vendors and family activities. Organizers describe the event as a celebration of local flavor, community spirit and the agricultural richness of the region, with every ticket helping fund Thrive's work.

Performers scheduled for Saturday include Chris Baker, Rhiannon Lace, the Doso Dirtbags and DJ Dale Young.

Corks & Shells debuted on Oct. 19, 2024, billed by organizers as Thrive's inaugural Wine and Pistachio Festival and a showcase for Southern New Mexico's pistachio and wine industries. From the start, Thrive said it intended the festival to become an annual fixture on the third weekend of October.

The festival returned to Alameda Park on Oct. 18, 2025, expanding its hours to 11 a.m. and pairing wines from local and regional vineyards with New Mexico pistachios, along with artisan, retail and food truck vendors.

This year's festival is presented in partnership with Visit Alamogordo and PNM.

Thrive in Southern New Mexico is an Alamogordo-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit that has served Otero and Lincoln counties since 1964. Its mission is "to advance the common good, create lasting change and enrich lives" by drawing on the compassion and resources of the community.

The organization funds local partner agencies through a multi-year community plan built around four goals: helping kids and families lead successful lives, improving health and independence, responding to emergency and basic needs, and encouraging civic and neighborhood involvement. Festivals like Corks & Shells help pay for that work.

item.title: Reeb’s Forced Resignation Exposes the Insider PAC Machine Propping Up John Block While Local Voters Are Left Behind
item.description:
Filings show the Clovis lawmaker gave $5,000 to Piñon PAC — more than 18 times what every Otero County resident gave it — as legislators from other districts supply nearly 90 percent of the committee’s money.

ALAMOGORDO — State Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) resigned her House seat on October 15, 2026, one day after a federal judge ruled that her simultaneous service as a legislator and a special prosecutor violated the separation-of-powers clause of the New Mexico Constitution.

The ruling came October 14 in Baldwin v. Morrissey, actor Alec Baldwin’s civil suit against the prosecutors who charged him in the 2021 “Rust” shooting. U.S. District Judge Kea Riggs dismissed many of Baldwin’s claims on prosecutorial immunity grounds but found that Reeb, who briefly served as a special prosecutor in the case, had exercised the power of two branches of state government at once. Reeb said she disagreed with the ruling but stepped down so she could keep prosecuting cases. She said she had relied on guidance from the State Ethics Commission and a 2024 Attorney General’s opinion. Records obtained by The Santa Fe New Mexican show she holds a 2024–2027 contract with the 9th Judicial District Attorney’s Office at $125 an hour, capped at $18,000 a month.

Within hours, Rep. John Block (R-Alamogordo) posted on X that Reeb was “one of the most talented lawmakers I’ve ever worked with” and that he was “proud to call her my friend.”

Campaign finance records show the relationship also runs through Block’s political action committee.

Reeb’s checks to Piñon PAC

Piñon PAC is the committee Block solicits for under his own name. Its filings with the Secretary of State show Reeb gave it $5,000 in three checks: $2,000 on January 27, 2025; $1,000 on October 6, 2025; and $2,000 on June 4, 2026.

The PAC’s registration lists Block as treasurer. Block’s own money has also moved through the PAC. His campaign committee, John for New Mexico, gave it $6,500 in 2024, and Block gave $2,000 personally in January 2025.

Money has also moved back out to Block. The PAC paid Block’s company, Piñon Post LLC, $2,336.90 on April 15, 2026, and another $2,336.90 on June 4, 2026. Both were described only as “Check,” with no purpose disclosed. The PAC also reimbursed Block $148.55 for stamps and gave $800 to his campaign in April 2025. The second payment to Piñon Post LLC was made the same day Reeb’s last $2,000 check was recorded. The filings do not show that one paid for the other.

Who funds the PAC

From January 2025 through June 2026, the most recent public filing, Piñon PAC raised $53,836.

Republican legislators from other districts: $47,148, or 87.6 percent. Sixteen House Republicans gave, including Reps. Terrazas, Vincent, Mason, Zamora, Pettigrew, Chatfield, Henry, Brown, Martinez, Baca, Montoya, Duncan, Jones and Reeb. House Republican Leader Gail Armstrong: $2,000. Armstrong publicly defended Reeb’s handling of her resignation on Friday. Otero County residents: $271, or one-half of one percent.

Reeb’s $5,000 alone was more than 18 times what every Otero County donor gave the PAC combined.

The PAC’s largest expenses were not in Otero County either. In 2025, a year with no election, it paid Right Insight LLC of Boise, Idaho, about $12,750 and Connector Labs Inc. of Frisco, Texas, $7,500, both described only as “consulting.” It reported $1,370 for a mailer in May 2026. Piñon PAC also mailed District 51 voters a flyer this month attacking Block’s opponent, independent Grace Nagamine, over her 2005–2008 record. Its cost will not appear until the next filing.

Block’s campaign: 0.4 percent from Otero County residents

The corporate donors were Chevron ($6,200), Permian Resources ($5,000), Devon Energy ($2,500), Presbyterian Health Plan ($1,000), Anheuser-Busch ($1,000) and Comcast ($500). The $104 from Otero County residents came from a single Alamogordo donor giving $10.41 a month.

The “big PAC” warning and the documented hypocrisy

In a recent fundraising email, Block told supporters he faces an opponent backed by a “deep-pocketed, far-left PAC” and asked for donations as small as $35.

Nagamine’s filings through June show no PAC contributions and her next filing will show a in kind contribution from a Tularosa based group. The Sierra Club’s Rio Grande Chapter endorsed her August 29. A Tularosa volunteer group says it has put about $2,000 of in-kind support into the race for her this month, which will appear in the next filing.

This further demonstrates the hypocrisy of the Block narrative to local constituents. More than 80 percent of the significant contributions to his campaign and nearly 90 percent of the money flowing into the PAC he controls come from out-of-county corporate, energy, PAC, and fellow-legislator sources. 

Local individual donors from Otero County account for well under 1 percent of both.

While Block asks grassroots supporters for $35 and $50 checks to fight phantom outside money, the public record shows Rep John Block is the one collecting it from Santa Fe insiders and corporate interests that do not live in District 51.

Nagamine has focused on the issues that affect District 51 residents—power bills, water infrastructure, veterans and military families, seniors, CYFD reform, and local economic needs—as laid out on her website and in her regular Facebook posts. 

Block continues to endorse and promote the self-interest of the energy companies, corporate donors, and allied PACs that fund his operation, while mailing personal attacks and warning of phantom outside money.

Block’s political operation is not powered by the people of Otero County.

It is powered by oil and corporate checks written from outside the district, by a network of House Republicans who do not live here and do not answer to local voters, and by a PAC that shares an address with his own company and writes checks back to it with no purpose disclosed.

Local residents are left to absorb the consequences of utility rate structures he opposed and infrastructure needs that remain unaddressed, while the money trail runs through Santa Fe and out-of-state firms.

The “big PAC” threat he describes in fundraising emails is the opposite of the one documented in the filings.

It is time to break the machine of special insider interests propping up Alamogordo’s political leadership with outsider money instead of the interests of the people who live here. 

On November 3, voters have a clear choice between a candidate who answers to local constituents on the issues that matter in this district and one whose campaign and PAC are sustained by the very outside money and insider network he claims to be fighting.

What's next

Reeb remains the only candidate on the ballot in House District 64. County commissioners in Chaves, Curry and Roosevelt counties are expected to send nominees to Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, who will appoint her successor.

Block faces Nagamine in House District 51 on Nov. 3. The next campaign finance reports will show fall fundraising and spending, including the cost of the PAC's October mailer.

Early voting had begun for many the call is to oust the incumbents and break the political machine that has stymied Alamogordo for decades.

item.title: In Memory of Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer
item.description:
Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer, age 94, passed away peacefully at her home in Alamogordo, New Mexico on Thursday, October 8, 2026.

Adelin was born in Carrizozo, New Mexico on August 22, 1932. She cherished her early years growing up on her family's ranch outside of town before moving to Truth or Consequences, New Mexico where she graduated from high school. She went on to attend Texas Tech University, earning a Bachelor of Business Administration degree.

Following college, Adelin moved to Roswell, New Mexico where she met and married William Carl "Bill" Schauer. Together they raised two children, Leda and Tony. The family eventually settled in High Rolls Mountain Park, New Mexico surrounded by tall pine trees, apple orchards, trout ponds, and winter snows.

Following Bill's passing and as her children established their careers, Adelin pursued further education, earning a counseling degree from CBN University. She then dedicated many years to serving the emotional and spiritual needs of her community. In later years, she moved down the mountain to Alamogordo where she happily spent the last two decades of her active life volunteering for political events, enjoying lunches with friends, and deepening her fellowship within the local Christian community.

Throughout her life, Adelin was a devoted servant leader, serving as the Southern New Mexico Area President of Women’s Aglow Fellowship, President of Alamogordo Republican Women, and sharing her musical talents as an organist and pianist while teaching Sunday school at various churches.

Adelin is survived by her son, Tony Schauer and his wife, Linda; her grandchildren, Jessica, Thomas, Sarah, Cheryl, and Robin; nine great grandchildren.

She was preceded in death by her husband, Bill Schauer; her daughter, Leda Schauer; her beloved brother, Dewey Stokes.

Services will be held at a later date.

item.title: Alamogordo Tigers Tigers Rally in Second Half to Beat Gadsden 23-14
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M- Alamogordo shook off a slow start Friday night, scoring three second-half touchdowns, including one on special teams, to beat Gadsden 23-14 in district play.

The win lifts the Tigers to 4-4 overall and 3-2 in district.

Gadsden struck first. With 9:22 left in the opening quarter, Rosalío Gomez hit Anthony Palomares on a 20-yard touchdown pass, and the extra point made it 7-0. That score held through the first quarter as Alamogordo's offense struggled to find a rhythm.

The Tigers got on the board late in the second quarter when Gabe Russell connected on a 36-yard field goal with 1:49 left. Gadsden took a 7-3 lead into halftime.

Alamogordo came out of the break with momentum. Nathanael Cereceres broke loose for a 42-yard touchdown run, and Russell's extra point gave the Tigers their first lead, 10-7, with 8:26 left in the third quarter.

The lead lasted less than a minute. On the next possession, Gadsden's Armando Ramirez answered with a 78-yard touchdown run, and the extra point put the visitors back in front 14-10 with 7:42 remaining in the quarter.

The Tigers' special teams then made the play of the night. With 31 seconds left in the third quarter, Tanner Nowaczck blocked a Gadsden punt and returned it 10 yards for a touchdown. Russell's kick made it 17-14 Alamogordo heading into the fourth..

Leyton Niland put the game out of reach midway through the final quarter with a 41-yard touchdown run at the 6:31 mark. The two-point try failed, but the Tigers' defense held the rest of the way to seal the 23-14 victory.

Alamogordo hosts Deming on Thursday.

Around the County

Tularosa 25, Capitan 6: The Wildcats improved to 5-3 and 1-1 in district. Tularosa hosts Legacy Academy next Friday.

Mesilla Valley Christian 50, Cloudcroft 0 (8-man): The Bears fell to 2-6 and 0-3 in district. Cloudcroft closes the regular season next Saturday at Mescalero Apache.

item.title: Tularosa school board tables policy revisions, approves Head Start agreement and equipment storage donation
item.description:
TULAROSA — The Tularosa Municipal Schools Board of Education on Wednesday, Oct. 14, put off action on three policy revisions tied to updated federal law, saying board members and the public need more time to review the proposed changes.

The board also approved an updated agreement with HELP New Mexico Head Start and accepted a community member's donation of a storage container to protect athletic equipment after thefts at the district's baseball and softball complex.

The superintendent recommended tabling three agenda items, including Policy Advisory No. 279, Commitment to Religious Neutrality. The New Mexico School Boards Association (NMSBA) Policy Service had recommended revisions to the three policies based on updated federal laws.

The superintendent said the recommended changes were redlined and attached to the agenda. "Just to ensure that you guys have time to really read over the proposed revisions, and to give time for public comment, I recommend tabling these three items for the next board meeting," the superintendent said.

Asked whether the changes would appear in student handbooks, the superintendent said the district's existing policies posted online would be updated. Any handbook language that conflicts with the revisions would also have to be changed. The board voted to table the items until its next meeting.

The board approved an updated memorandum of understanding with HELP New Mexico Head Start. The revision adds transportation to the agreement. HELP New Mexico now provides after-school supervision for students who need it.

The agreement also covers the district's half-day 3-year-old students, who will be transported to HELP New Mexico when their half-day program ends. The organization serves children ages 3 to 12, including kindergarten through fifth grade. The superintendent said the agreement carries no financial terms; it sets out who is responsible for enrollment and transportation.

The board accepted a community member's offer to donate a concrete pad and a C-can storage container at the baseball and softball complex. The superintendent said the area has had thefts and that equipment kept there includes a costly pitching machine.

The container would sit between the pitching cage and the existing concession stand and serve both baseball and softball. One board member noted that teams now haul equipment back and forth each day to keep it from being stolen. Board members asked that the container be painted within the next year to match existing structures at the complex.

The board approved the meeting agenda, the minutes of its Sept. 9 meeting and the September 2026 check register. No opposing votes were heard on any item.

In the superintendent's report, district schools reported gains in attendance and family engagement through the first nine weeks.

Tularosa Intermediate School raised its attendance rate from 90.8% last year to 93%. The school has set up a process to reach students who miss school regularly and will have its houses compete for the best attendance. The superintendent credited the school's Native American liaison with communicating with parents and getting students to class. The state Public Education Department's Safe and Healthy Schools Bureau has approved the school's attendance improvement plan.

TIS hosted Tularosa Middle School's STEAM Night, which drew more than 100 parents and family members. The school is also launching a student leadership group called Wildcat ROAR, focused on anti-bullying, conflict resolution and respect for others.

Tularosa High School reported 92% attendance overall for the first nine weeks, with seniors posting a personal-best 98%. Last week the school topped its 95% attendance goal. Reported incidents dropped from 24 in September to nine so far in October.

Sophomores took the PSAT last week. Because the high school runs on a block schedule, students are already taking middle-of-the-year math and English language arts assessments, with the STAR test to follow in November. Counselor Mrs. Coleman has met with every senior for credit checks and post-high-school planning.

The superintendent also noted a problem with senior portraits from Lifetouch. The company is working with each parent who reaches out to fix it.

Tularosa Middle School completed 127 parent-teacher conferences, which the superintendent called a record. Staff are working through 90-day improvement plans in English language arts and math, using assessment data to guide reteaching and intervention. A new Choices Matter program uses lunch detention to teach responsibility, decision-making and self-control.

Tularosa Elementary School is partnering with the high school's Educators Rising class, which places high school students in classrooms and sends them to read to younger students monthly. Middle school leadership students are mentoring kindergartners and first graders at lunch on skills like taking turns and following directions. This month, students caught doing something kind can earn "Be Boo-tiful" tickets, with prize drawings on Thursdays.

Football has begun district play and was scheduled to host Capitan on Friday, Oct. 16, for Senior Night. Volleyball hosted Hatch on Oct. 15 and opens district play against Dexter on Tuesday, Oct. 20. Middle school volleyball and football have wrapped up their seasons. Middle school basketball begins Nov. 2, and high school basketball begins Nov. 16.

The district has set Thursday, Nov. 5, for a topping-out ceremony on its construction project, marking placement of the final beam on the structure. The construction company plans a cookout and will invite the village and other dignitaries. The time has not been announced; the superintendent said more information will follow. The board plans to post a notice of a possible quorum for the event.

It’s  reported that staff finished training on the district's new cloud-based business system, which rolls out next week. School secretaries are already entering requisitions in it, cutting down on paper. She said the district has met twice in recent weeks with its food service provider and that the transition is going smoothly.

Board members discussed attending the NMSBA annual conference Dec. 3–5 in Albuquerque. Members also noted that NMSBA now offers online options for completing required board training hours.

item.title: "Frozen" Dazzles at the Flickinger as Children's Music Theater Opens Season in Grand Style
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — With the staggering vocal talents of Isabella Ochoa and Kendall Kunihiro (aka Elsa and Anna) leading the way, "Frozen: The Broadway Musical" from the Children's Music Theater of Alamogordo opened Friday, Oct. 16, at the Flickinger Center for Performing Arts. 

Impressive sets, costumes, special effects and a live orchestra set the stage for stellar performances by a large cast of kids ages 7 to 17. Favorites like "Let It Go," "Do You Want to Build a Snowman?" and "Love Is an Open Door" drew some of the night's biggest cheers. Behind the scenes, a student stage crew kept Arendelle running smoothly.

A cast that shines from top to bottom

Ochoa commanded the stage as Elsa, balancing the queen's icy reserve with real vulnerability. Her voice filled the hall, and her "Let It Go" brought the audience to its feet with a moment of pure goosebumps.

Kunihiro was a delight as Anna, bursting with warmth, comic timing and a voice that soared in every number. Her chemistry with Ochoa made the sisters' bond the true heart of the show.

Eric Balogh gave Kristoff an easygoing charm and a rugged, likable presence, while Caleb Cooper's Sven, the loyal reindeer, earned laughs and affection without saying a word. Together they were one of the evening's most endearing pairings.

Kylie Kunihiro was a scene-stealer as Olaf. Her sunny energy and perfect comic instincts had the youngest audience members giggling and the grown-ups laughing right along with them.

Caleb Crabtree played Hans with smooth charisma that made his turn all the more satisfying, and Gavin Shepherd hammed it up wonderfully as the scheming Duke of Weselton, drawing laughs with every pompous entrance.

The younger performers were a highlight in their own right. Elizabeth Reuter and Olivia Calles were adorable and affecting as Young Elsa and Young Anna, setting up the story's emotional stakes with real tenderness. Olivia Davison and Evelyn George carried the sisters' journey forward beautifully as Middle Elsa and Middle Anna.

Trent Hileman's Oaken brought a cheerful, crowd-pleasing burst of fun, and Samuel Thrasher and Addison Gilliland gave King Agnarr and Queen Iduna a gentle dignity that made the royal family's story land. Asher Celoria as Pabbie and Valerie Garcia as Bulda brought warmth and humor to the hidden folk.

The 26-member ensemble deserves its own standing ovation. Whether as villagers, courtiers or hidden folk, they filled every scene with energy, tight harmonies and sharp choreography, giving the production the full, rich sound of a professional company.

A story within the story

For Ochoa, the role meant more than a starring turn. She is a cancer survivor, and her portrayal of a young woman who stops hiding and embraces her strength gave the show's message of courage and self-acceptance special weight for everyone who knows her story.

Among those congratulating her after the curtain call was Grace Nagamine, candidate for New Mexico House District 51. Despite a busy schedule, Nagamine made a point of being there to celebrate Ochoa's victory over cancer and her starring role, and posed for photos with the young star in full Elsa costume.

"My schedule was packed, but I could not miss the chance to see this beautiful young girl shine," Nagamine said. "To watch her thrive as a survivor and take the stage as Elsa was something special. She is an inspiration to us all.

What's next

Director and CMTA co-founder Heather Bash used the evening to announce what's next: the program's Spring 2027 production will be "The Sound of Music," with auditions set for January.

Remaining performances: today, Sunday, Oct. 18 at 2 p.m., and Friday and Saturday, Oct. 23 and 24 at 7 p.m. Tickets are available through the Flickinger Center for Performing Arts.

item.title: Otero County’s early vote follows statewide shifts as legislative races head into the final two weeks
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026

Early voting in New Mexico House District 51 has settled into a slow, steady pace after a busy opening day, and county ballot data show hundreds of voters who requested mail ballots have yet to return them. With 16 days until Election Day, the numbers also show Otero County moving in step with statewide trends, even as its voters lean differently than the rest of New Mexico.

Through Oct. 16, District 51 had received 1,962 ballots: 1,497 cast in person and 465 returned by mail. Republicans account for 847 of those ballots (43%), Democrats 775 (40%) and voters who decline to state a party 329 (17%). A handful came from Libertarian, Green and other minor-party voters.

The race pits Republican incumbent John Block, who has held the seat since 2023, against independent Grace A. Nagamine, a lifelong Alamogordo resident and founder of Royal Angels. Nagamine has said she is running as an independent because the district’s problems, including an aging water system, child-welfare reform and housing for military families, are not partisan issues.

Opening-day rush has faded

In-person voting opened Oct. 6 with 263 ballots cast in the district, the busiest day so far. Daily totals have since held between about 115 and 190, with the low point of 114 on Oct. 12, Indigenous Peoples’ Day. Expanded early voting at the Otero County Fairgrounds began Oct. 17, and county officials and campaigns will be watching whether the second site lifts the numbers.

In-person voters have leaned Republican: 739 Republicans, 500 Democrats and 250 decline-to-state voters through Oct. 16. Mail ballots show the opposite pattern, with 275 returned by Democrats compared with 108 by Republicans and 79 by independents.

How District 51 compares with the state

Statewide, about 63,000 New Mexicans had voted early or by absentee ballot as of Oct. 16, roughly 4.3% of registered voters, according to Secretary of State data reported by Source NM. Democrats cast nearly 37,000 of those ballots, Republicans about 17,000 and independents nearly 9,000.

District 51’s early electorate runs about 16 points more Republican than the state’s, and independents make up a slightly larger share locally. But the direction of travel is the same. Statewide, the Republican share of in-person early votes has climbed from about 26% in the first days to about 30%. In District 51, the Republican share of in-person votes rose from 47.5% over the first four days to 51% over the next five, while the Democratic share slipped from 35% to 32% and the decline-to-state share from 17% to 16%.

The two parties read those numbers differently. The Democratic Party of New Mexico told the Santa Fe New Mexican that its voters are performing well even by Democratic standards. Republican Party of New Mexico spokesperson Leticia Muñoz said Republicans traditionally turn out on Election Day and predicted the numbers would shift once expanded early voting began.

New Mexico’s 2022 midterm turnout was 52.4% of registered voters, and the state has added about 94,000 voters since then. Bernalillo County Clerk Michelle Kavanaugh told the Albuquerque Journal she expects turnout to be up this year, following a June primary that drew near-record participation.

The national picture

Nationally, more than 700,000 Americans in at least 30 states had voted by Oct. 1, according to reporting citing CNN data. Democrats were requesting mail ballots at higher rates than at the same point in 2024 in several states with major races, including Iowa, where Democrats made up 67% of requests, up from 54%. Analysts caution that early returns skew toward older and mail voters, and that Republicans have increasingly shifted to voting in person, a pattern that District 51’s split between mail and in-person ballots reflects.

801 ballots still outstanding

Of the mail ballots sent to District 51 voters, 801 had not been returned as of Oct. 16. Democrats hold 393 of them, Republicans 226 and decline-to-state voters 175, with seven more held by minor-party voters. Mailed ballots must reach the county clerk by 7 p.m. on Election Day to be counted.

“[DRAFT QUOTE — PENDING CAMPAIGN APPROVAL] Every ballot that comes back early is a voice already heard. If you have a ballot on your kitchen table, fill it out and drop it off this week. If you’d rather vote in person, the Fairgrounds is open now. Don’t wait for Election Day — District 51’s future is being decided right now,” said a spokesperson for the Nagamine campaign.

What the trends mean for each local race

House District 51: John Block (R) vs. Grace A. Nagamine (I)

As the district with the most Otero County voters, District 51 has cast about two-thirds of the county’s early ballots. A rising Republican share of in-person votes mirrors the statewide shift. For an independent candidate, the 175 unreturned decline-to-state ballots and the 393 unreturned Democratic ballots are the largest pool of votes still in voters’ hands, while the incumbent’s party is gaining ground in person.

House District 53: Ben Luna Jr. (R) vs. Sarah Silva (D, incumbent)

District 53 is centered in eastern Doña Ana County and reaches only a corner of Otero County around Chaparral, so local numbers are small: an earlier county snapshot showed 28 ballots received from the Otero portion and 77 mail ballots outstanding. An early voting site at the Chaparral Far South Fire Station, 827 Luna St., opens Oct. 29. Because most of the district’s voters live in Doña Ana County, where Democratic early voting tends to be strong, the statewide pattern is likely to matter more here than Otero County’s.

House District 54: Johnathan Allen Henry (R), unopposed

With no opponent on the ballot, District 54’s outcome is settled, but its voters still help decide the Senate District 33, governor and congressional races. The county snapshot showed 642 ballots received from the district’s Otero County portion and 302 mail ballots outstanding.

House District 56: Harlan Vincent (R, incumbent)

District 56 spans Lincoln and Otero counties. The county snapshot showed 444 ballots received from its Otero County portion and 218 mail ballots outstanding. An early voting site at the Inn of the Mountain Gods in Mescalero is scheduled for Oct. 28 through 30.

Senate District 33: William Griffin (D) vs. Rex Wilson (R)

The only state Senate seat on the 2026 ballot covers parts of Otero, Lincoln and Chaves counties, all areas where Republicans have historically led early voting. If the statewide drift toward Republican in-person voting continues, it is likely to show up most strongly in districts like this one. The nearly 1,400 mail ballots still outstanding across Otero County could still shape the margin.

Other races on the ballot

• County Commission: Republican Christopher Wayne Glidden vs. Democrat Alan David Gonzalez in District 1; Republican Jonathan T. Emery vs. independent Evan Christopher Lambert in District 2.• Governor: Democrat Deb Haaland vs. Republican Gregg Hull.• U.S. Senate: Democrat Ben Ray Luján vs. Republican Larry Marker. U.S. House District 2: Democrat Gabe Vasquez vs. Republican Gregory Cunningham.• Four constitutional amendments, three statewide bond questions and a local Otero County bond.

How to vote early

• Tuesday, Oct. 20 is the last day to request an absentee ballot.• Otero County Administration Building, 1101 N. New York Ave., Room 101: weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. through Oct. 31.• Otero County Fairgrounds, 401 Fairgrounds Road: Oct. 17 through Oct. 31. Call the clerk to confirm hours.• Inn of the Mountain Gods, Mescalero: Oct. 28–30. Chaparral Far South Fire Station: Oct. 29–31.• Same-day registration is available at early-voting sites and on Election Day.• Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., and any Otero County voter may use any voting convenience center.

Questions can be directed to the Otero County Clerk’s Office at (575) 437-4942 or nmvote.org.

item.title: Rardin Didn’t Ask, Didn’t Know: City Leaders Cast Doubt on Downtown Projects Without Checking First
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M- Two downtown business owners say they were publicly attacked at the most recent Alamogordo City Commission meeting by a commissioner who never contacted them, has never visited their properties and does not represent their district. They say his remarks were wrong, damaging and defamatory. Former City Manager Dr. Hernandez, who recommended both projects, is also disputing how the meeting described them.

The owners of the White Sands Theater and Rad Retrocade have each received Local Economic Development Act (LEDA) funding. Both told Alamogordo Town News that their projects are moving forward and that they are in full compliance with their agreements with the city. According to Hernandez, each owner plans to put more than $1 million of their own money into their building. The owners say what they got in return was a public suggestion from the dais that they had taken the city’s money and done nothing.

The exchange

The discussion came up under an agenda item on allocating the city’s remaining LEDA funds. Commissioner Josh Rardin pointed to the two projects.

https://youtube.com/shorts/9fvl_hPLwIU?is=m-rWi59pnBAZk8eu

“The ones down there on New York Avenue we gave money to, I haven’t seen any action on either of them,” Rardin said.“In the event that they don’t do anything with them, what is our recourse? Do we call that back or…”

City Manager Robert Stockwell did not correct the premise. He went further. “Well, we can try,” he said, adding that it“baffled” him that the city would “give a million dollars to somebody before there’s bills to pay.” He said “the White Sands Theater got a million dollar check. We don’t know where that money is.” The discussion then raised the possibility that there would be “nothing to claw back” and that the city could end up with “one more derelict building.”The two downtown projects were discussed in the same breath as Sunbaked Biscuits, which Stockwell described as a complete default on a $1.9 million project.

No one at the meeting offered any evidence that either downtown project had stalled or broken its agreement. According to the owners, no one had asked them.

Former city manager: “inaccurate”

Hernandez was city manager when both LEDA agreements were approved. In a statement, Hernandez said they were“deeply disappointed by the Commission meeting’s characterization of downtown revitalization.”

“The claim that funding was provided without bills having been paid is inaccurate. So is the claim that nothing is happening downtown,” Hernandez said. “Troy and Alex submitted invoices and status updates, with plans involving more than $1 million of their own investment in each building.”

Hernandez also confirmed what both owners told Alamogordo Town News: no one at the meeting had talked to them first. “To my knowledge, only the mayor and I have reached out to them,” Hernandez said. “Public funding deserves scrutiny. That scrutiny requires accurate information and direct communication.”

Hernandez noted that the projects were the commission’s decision, not a city manager acting alone. “I only recommended; the Commission approved. It is no secret the Commissioners were willing to push back when they disagreed. But both were approved unanimously. I stand by my recommendations.”

The agreements were drafted under Hernandez and the city attorney at the time, using the state’s LEDA template, as the state recommends.

“The approach is the same. The location is different.”

Hernandez also pointed out a contradiction. Stockwell has been promoting creative public-private partnerships to deal with deteriorating properties on 10th Street. That is the same strategy, Hernandez said, that the city used downtown.

“Mr. Stockwell’s proposed solutions for 10th Street, addressing deteriorating properties through creative public-private partnerships, are exactly what we pursued downtown. The approach is the same. The location is different,” Hernandez said.

“I agree that 10th Street needs attention. Downtown did too. Perhaps its beauty today makes its former condition easy to forget. Mr. Stockwell may not have seen it then, or have all the correct information, but the Commission did.”Hernandez said those conditions led the commission to approve the downtown Metropolitan Redevelopment Area (MRA) in 2019 and to back its redevelopment.

That effort combined state grants, city investment, MainStreet partnerships and private investment from businesses including Ink Well, Rad Retrocade, the White Sands Theater and Pymo.

“Different priorities are understandable,” Hernandez said.“Praising an approach for 10th Street while disparaging that same approach downtown is unfortunate. Casting doubt on the business owners who invested significantly here undermines the very partnerships the City Manager now says it wants to build.”

“Uninformed”

When Alamogordo Town News contacted Stockwell after the meeting, he acknowledged he was “uninformed of the status of the two properties.” He said he had been trying to explain to the commission that the city’s options would be limited if a project ever failed, because the agreements have limited reporting requirements, and that he did not like the contracts.

That leaves a public discussion of possible clawbacks against two local businesses, held by a city manager who says he did not know the status of their projects and a commissioner who, according to both owners, never picked up the phone. Meanwhile, the former city manager says the invoices and status updates had already been submitted.

Not his district, and no phone call

Neither property is in Rardin’s district. Both owners told Alamogordo Town News that Rardin made no attempt to call, meet with or visit them before he spoke at the meeting. They said neither Rardin nor Stockwell has ever asked for a walkthrough or a progress update.

Rardin has described himself as a contractor. Anyone in construction knows that the early stages of a major renovation, such as roofing, demolition, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, security and architectural design, happen mostly out of sight. A building that looks unchanged from the sidewalk is not a building where nothing is happening.

Rad Retrocade: in compliance, opening spring 2027

Alex, the owner of Rad Retrocade, said he has submitted receipts to the city and met with city engineer Shelly Barron several months ago, and that the project is in full compliance with its agreement.

Extensive work has already been done inside the building, he said. New air conditioning units have been ordered. Significant equipment and arcade games for the mezzanine are in local storage, and work continues on the electrical, plumbing and other systems. More exterior work will be visible starting in December, and the arcade remains on track to open in spring 2027, as promised.

Alex said he was upset by the exchange, which he considers an attack on his business, and has contacted an attorney about the comments.

White Sands Theater: new roof, new wiring and a theft along the way

Troy, the owner of the White Sands Theater, also owns three operating businesses, including the German restaurant on New York Avenue. He told Alamogordo Town News he was angered by the commission’s remarks and has sent a scathing letter to the mayor and city manager. He says the project is in full compliance with its agreement.

The theater’s latest renovation update shows a project that has been working through serious obstacles:

The old fly loft on the roof has been removed, and a new roof is on the building.The back storage room door and window have been sealed with concrete to stop break-ins.Thieves broke in and stole a large portion of the building’s copper electrical wiring.The owners have contracted to upgrade and replace the electrical system to support the theater’s new digital equipment.A contractor hired to redo the exterior stucco took the owners’ deposit and disappeared. A new contractor has been hired, and the owners plan to take legal action to recover the deposit.An architect is designing the interior layout, which will slightly change the building’s footprint.

“Progress takes time, but we can’t wait to show you what’s coming together,” the owners wrote.

What comes next

The city’s first formal check on the LEDA projects is expected in December. Both owners say they welcome it. They want to know why that check-in didn’t happen before their businesses were questioned in a public meeting.

Alamogordo Town News will continue to follow both projects.

item.title: In Memory of Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer
item.description:
Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer, age 94, passed away peacefully at her home in Alamogordo, New Mexico on Thursday, October 8, 2026.

Adelin was born in Carrizozo, New Mexico on August 22, 1932. She cherished her early years growing up on her family's ranch outside of town before moving to Truth or Consequences, New Mexico where she graduated from high school. She went on to attend Texas Tech University, earning a Bachelor of Business Administration degree.

Following college, Adelin moved to Roswell, New Mexico where she met and married William Carl "Bill" Schauer. Together they raised two children, Leda and Tony. The family eventually settled in High Rolls Mountain Park, New Mexico surrounded by tall pine trees, apple orchards, trout ponds, and winter snows.

Following Bill's passing and as her children established their careers, Adelin pursued further education, earning a counseling degree from CBN University. She then dedicated many years to serving the emotional and spiritual needs of her community. In later years, she moved down the mountain to Alamogordo where she happily spent the last two decades of her active life volunteering for political events, enjoying lunches with friends, and deepening her fellowship within the local Christian community.

Throughout her life, Adelin was a devoted servant leader, serving as the Southern New Mexico Area President of Women’s Aglow Fellowship, President of Alamogordo Republican Women, and sharing her musical talents as an organist and pianist while teaching Sunday school at various churches.

Adelin is survived by her son, Tony Schauer and his wife, Linda; her grandchildren, Jessica, Thomas, Sarah, Cheryl, and Robin; nine great grandchildren.

She was preceded in death by her husband, Bill Schauer; her daughter, Leda Schauer; her beloved brother, Dewey Stokes.

Services will be held at a later date.
